title: Usability requirement gathering and specification

sentences.text: Hello and welcome to the NPTEL MOOCs course on Foundations for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems.
So, we are discussing requirement gathering for end users for our XR systems, and we will continue our discussion in this part of the lecture as well.
So, earlier we talked about the importance of gathering end user requirements.
which is to ensure usability of the system, which is a very important concern when we are talking about XR systems as these are part of interactive systems.
We also started our discussion on a method of usability requirement gathering that is called contextual inquiry.
So, we are going to continue our discussion on contextual inquiry.

So, earlier we have learned what contextual inquiry is, that is to observe users in their natural work setting, observe targeted groups of users or specified groups of users in their natural work setting to understand how they behave and what they do.
Now let us see what the different ways contextual inquiry can be performed are.
So there are broadly two ways for performing contextual inquiry.
One is the active mode.
In this mode, the observer or the person who is performing the contextual inquiry is physically present in the environment where the users are doing their tasks.
There is another passive mode; here user activities are recorded or videotaped and So, there is no observer as such, but the activities are recorded and then observed later by the observer.
If there are some issues, those can be clarified through interaction with the users.
One important thing here is that during the inquiry, the observer should act as an apprentice, and treat the users as masters.
So, this is called the master apprentice model.
The purpose is to learn the user behavior, not to teach users how to behave.
So, it is not easy.
We often get this behavioral trait that whenever somebody is doing something, we often get the urge to tell the user, okay, do not do it in this way, do it in that way, that will be better for you.
That type of advisory is not desirable.
In fact, these are prohibited when you are trying to perform a genuine contextual inquiry.
So, ideally you should always assume that you are the learner and the users are the teachers.
So, they are teaching you how they behave and how typically users would be behaving in a given context and you will learn that behavior from them rather than trying to teach them how to behave.
So, that is about different categories.
Now, let us talk about the stages of the contextual inquiry.
So there are five stages.
These stages are basically a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.
First is plan, then initiate, execute, close, and reflect.
So the inquiry starts with the plan stage.
It goes to the initiate stage, then the actual inquiry takes place in the execute stage.
Then it is closed, and then finally reflect means analyzing the data.
So in the plan stage, what are the things to do typically?
Plan, as the name suggests, means planning the activities.
So, we first start with identification of the goals of observation, what we are trying to observe.
That needs to be first identified.
Otherwise, if we directly reach there, reach into the workplace, and try to start observing, then we will be confused about what to actually observe.
So, first you plan for what exactly we are trying to observe.
The second part is gathering knowledge about the task domain.
So, what kind of task domain, how the domain is organized, all these things need to be known.
Also, plan for arrangements for recording observations if required, or noting down observations, how to do that; all these things need to be planned.
An essential part of the planning is the identification of the users, and the date, time, and place of the observation.

Certainly this is one of the most essential components of the plan stage and it always helps to have a script of the procedure and rehearse the script so that on the day of observation it goes as per plan.
So scripting of the procedure always helps.
In the initiate stage, that is the second stage, We should contact the authorities for permissions, all necessary permissions, because we will be observing the employees in their work setting.
And open communication with the end users to remove their anxieties.
So, end users often believe that these observations may lead to something bad for them.
So, we need to remove those anxieties so that they can behave naturally in their workplace.
Obtaining permission is also very important because you are going to observe them in their workplace.
So, all necessary permissions from relevant authorities must be obtained beforehand.
The execute test stage is the one where we actually perform the observation.
So, performing observations and recording data takes place in the execute stage.
In the close stage, ideally we should convey our gratitude by sending thank you notes to the users including the authorities maybe.
Why?
Because in the future you may need to conduct such activities again or some subsequent testing activities maybe usability testing activities where such users may be useful.
So, it is always a good idea to formally close by sending thank you notes or some sort of message conveying how they helped you and how grateful you are for the service provided by them.
So, these types of things turn out to be quite useful in the future.
Finally, comes the reflect stage.
In this stage, the observer or the experimental team analyzes the data which has been collected during the execute stage and identifies the design goals.
Now, this is not an easy stage, this is not a very easy thing to do.
Because there can be lots of data.
So data are essentially the kind of notes you are taking or the kind of things you are doing.
So this amount of data can be huge and sorting them, trying to find patterns from them, trying to find goals from them is not easy.
You can do it manually of course, entirely based on your skill.
However, there are some tools and techniques available which often help.

One such useful technique is called the affinity diagram method, which is a way to arrange the data so as to find out a pattern from the data easily, which leads to the design specification of the design goals.
So, let us try to have a quick look at the affinity diagram method.
what it is and how it can be used.
Now, when we talk about this affinity diagram method, this is essentially a method to analyze the data collected through contextual inquiry.
It consists of five steps.
Generate ideas, step number one.
Display ideas, two.
Sort ideas into groups, step number three.
Create the group header or provide some names, identifiers to the group, and finally draw the finished diagram.
So, these are the five steps of the affinity diagram method.
Let us try to understand these five steps in terms of one example.
Let us assume that we are building a class note-taking application.

Then there is one app notion: a web application and Xournal++ and desktop software.
So we collected data assuming that the users are using either of these methods and we noted their behavior.
So, the observations during the contextual inquiry were noted down and subsequently analyzed using the five stages of the affinity diagram method.

So, ideas are generated means notes taken, and then maybe when a note is taken during observation, that may be refined with better language in subsequent processing.
So, idea generation refers to the final note That is taken by the observer, and then once those are put together in a place, it can be a wall, it can be a board, anything that is called the display.
So, stage 1 and 2 refer to idea generation and display.
Then these notes are moved around so that they fall into a certain pattern, which we are calling sorting into groups with a pattern defining the members of each group.
Then what we are doing is assigning some header to the groups.
Now, this header is essentially referring to the pattern which binds the ideas within a group.
So, navigation in notebook, navigation in notes.
or note organization, all these are headers.
Note that these were not there in the initial ideas, but this came after the ideas were gone through, ideas were understood, ideas were moved around to organize.

Final drawing is essentially sorting all the ideas into groups.
Say for example, navigating in notebooks, media content, navigating in notes, note organization, text formatting, storage and privacy.
These six can be the header part.
And we can see that all the notes that we have taken we can organize them neatly under the six headers.
Say navigation in notebook comprises three ideas or notes.

Navigation in note two ideas.
Note organization again two ideas.
Text formatting, 4 ideas.
Finally, storage and privacy, 3 ideas.
So, essentially the total 19 ideas that we have seen earlier, we can organize into these 6 groups.
The number of ideas in each group can vary significantly.

Now, as you can understand while observing we take notes, but later on, repositioning or sorting the notes under clear headers is the most challenging task which we need to do here for further analysis the data or usage of the data.
So, after that final drawing, what we do is reflection.
Reflection means what to do with the data.
So, we can come up with a set of design recommendations based on the data.
In our specific example about note-taking application based on the six groups, we can say that for correcting mistakes, there should be a provision to erase content.
This would help in keeping the notes neat and tidy.
So, this guideline, we can call it a guideline or recommendation.

parts.objective: Describe the two modes and core principles of performing contextual inquiry for gathering usability requirements

key_points.text: Contextual inquiry is a method that involves observing specific groups of users in their natural work setting to understand their behavior.
Contextual inquiry can be executed in two ways: an active mode or a passive mode.
Active mode of contextual inquiry requires the observer to be physically present in the user's environment while they are completing tasks.
During contextual inquiry, the observer must follow the master-apprentice model, meaning the observer should act as a learner who observes user behavior rather than attempting to teach them.

terms.name: Contextual inquiry
terms.definition: Contextual inquiry is a method used to understand user behavior by observing targeted groups of users in their natural work setting.

terms.name: Passive mode
terms.definition: Passive mode is a method of contextual inquiry where user activities are recorded or videotaped for later observation by the observer, meaning no observer is physically present during the activity.

terms.name: Master apprentice model
terms.definition: Master apprentice model is a model for contextual inquiry where the observer acts as an apprentice and treats the users as masters to learn user behavior rather than teaching them how to behave.

parts.objective: Describe the five stages of contextual inquiry and detail the steps necessary during the planning stage

key_points.text: The contextual inquiry process is a systematic method consisting of five stages: Plan, Initiate, Execute, Close, and Reflect.
The initial phase of planning requires identifying the specific goals of the observation to ensure focus and prevent confusion.
Key point: "During the planning stage, researchers must gather knowledge about the task domain and identify the users." (cited sentences)
It is essential to script and rehearse the procedure beforehand so that the observation day proceeds exactly as planned.

terms.name: Contextual inquiry
terms.definition: Contextual inquiry is an inquiry process consisting of five stages that provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry.

terms.name: Plan stage
terms.definition: The plan stage is the first stage of a contextual inquiry where activities are organized. This stage involves identifying what to observe, gathering knowledge about the task domain, and planning for recordings, users, and the observation timeline.

terms.name: Task domain
terms.definition: The task domain refers to the area of activity being studied, and planning requires comprehensive knowledge of what kind of domain it is and how it is organized.

parts.objective: Identify the stages of usability research, from initiation to reflection, and apply the five steps of the affinity diagram method

key_points.text: Before observing employees, all necessary permissions must be obtained from authorities and open communication is needed to remove end-user anxieties.,,
Data collected during the execute stage can be massive, making the task of sorting them and finding patterns difficult.,
The affinity diagram method is a useful technique for analyzing data collected through contextual inquiry to find patterns and define design goals.,
The affinity diagram method consists of five steps: Generate ideas, Display ideas, Sort ideas into groups, Create group headers, and Draw the finished diagram.,,,,

terms.name: Initiate stage
terms.definition: Initiate stage is the second stage of the process where researchers contact relevant authorities for permissions and maintain open communication with end users to remove their anxieties.

terms.name: Execute stage
terms.definition: Execute stage is the stage where the actual observation takes place and the experimental team records the resulting data.

terms.name: Close stage
terms.definition: Close stage is the stage where the team conveys gratitude by sending thank you notes to users and authorities to facilitate potential future testing activities.

terms.name: Reflect stage
terms.definition: Reflect stage is the final stage where the observer or experimental team analyzes the data collected during the execute stage to identify design goals.

terms.name: Affinity diagram method
terms.definition: Affinity diagram method is a technique used to arrange collected data to easily identify patterns, which leads to the design specification of design goals.

parts.objective: Apply the affinity diagram method to transform raw user observations into meaningful usability design recommendations

key_points.text: Contextual inquiry gathers data on usability requirements by observing user behavior using different tools (e.g., physical paper, Notion, Xournal++).
The affinity diagram method involves five stages: generating ideas (notes from observations), displaying them, sorting them into groups, providing a header for each group, and final reflection.
Sorting ideas into groups involves identifying patterns (e.g., 'organization of notes') among similar observations.
After sorting and creating headers, the final reflection step uses the grouped data to formulate specific design recommendations for the system.
Using contextual inquiry ensures that design choices are informed by actual users' needs and expectations, unlike uninformed design choices.

terms.name: Contextual inquiry
terms.definition: Contextual inquiry is a method used to gather data that is supposed to be usability requirements. The data collected through this method is analyzed to provide information for design choices.

terms.name: Affinity diagram method
terms.definition: The affinity diagram method is a multi-stage process used to analyze and structure raw user observations by first generating and displaying ideas, and then sorting them into meaningful groups.

terms.surface: sorting of the ideas into groups
terms.name: Sorting into groups
terms.definition: Sorting into groups is the process of identifying patterns among raw ideas and grouping together similar ideas based on shared characteristics. This step involves moving notes around until they fall into a pattern that defines the members of each group.

terms.name: Content management
terms.definition: Content management is a common idea or pattern that relates issues such as the difficulty in erasing content or the inability to relocate content.

terms.name: Header
terms.definition: A header is a name or title provided after the ideas are grouped, which identifies the underlying pattern or theme that links all the ideas within that group.

terms.name: Idea
terms.definition: An idea is essentially a note taken by an observer during a study, which may later be refined during subsequent processing steps.

terms.name: Affinity diagram
terms.definition: The affinity diagram is a process framework used to categorize and relate raw notes taken from user observations, where each note is called an idea.

terms.name: Idea generation
terms.definition: Idea generation refers to the creation of the final note taken by the observer, which serves as the raw input data for subsequent analysis.

terms.name: Reflection
terms.definition: Reflection is a process carried out after organizing collected data, involving determining what actions should be taken with that data.

parts.objective: Differentiate between identifying usability requirements and prescribing implementation details

key_points.text: Requirement gathering focuses on identifying *what* needs to be usable, not providing a prescription for how to implement it.
The process following data collection (CI) involves analyzing and reflecting upon the findings.
Usability requirements can be gathered following a five-stage process: plan, initiated, executed, closed, and reflected.
The affinity diagram method is used during the reflection stage of data analysis.

terms.name: Contextual inquiry
terms.definition: Contextual Inquiry is a method used to collect usability requirements, and it follows five stages: plan, initiated the process, executed or collected the data, closed, and reflect.

terms.name: Affinity diagram method
terms.definition: The Affinity Diagram Method is a tool used to perform data analysis or the reflection stage after usability data has been collected.

parts.objective: Apply the Affinity Diagram process by generating, grouping, and naming user ideas based on observation data

key_points.text: Affinity diagram involves five stages: generate idea, display idea, sort, create group header, and draw the finished diagram.
Initial user ideas are collected and noted down using sticky notes during observation periods.
Key point: "The process begins by generating and displaying ideas collected from user observations." (cited sentences)
Ideas can be organized into related groups, and each group is given a descriptive header.

terms.name: Affinity diagram
terms.definition: An affinity diagram is a tool that comprises several stages: generating ideas, displaying ideas, sorting, creating, grouping headers, and finally drawing the finished diagram for analysis.

terms.name: Group header
terms.definition: Group header is a specific label used in an affinity diagram to summarize a cluster of related ideas into a shared theme, such as 'reminder setting' or 'work scheduling'.

parts.objective: Refine observational data gathered from Contextual Inquiry by grouping and structuring findings to move toward system specifications

key_points.text: Observed data can be refined and divided into logical subgroups, such as separating overall scheduling from day-wise scheduling.
When analyzing user observations, there is no single, unique way to perform the grouping.
Reflective observation data can be converted from ideas into actionable guidelines and implementable specifications.

terms.name: Contextual inquiry
terms.definition: Contextual inquiry is a method for gathering requirements. It is a process for which the lecture covers the basic idea, how it is used, and how to analyze the data.

terms.name: Requirement gathering
terms.definition: Requirement gathering is a basic idea discussed in the lecture. It is a subject explored alongside contextual inquiry as a method for gathering.
